subject: Banking
title: Will Banks Ever Clean Up?
description: A short lesson to help you apply Will Banks Ever Clean Up?.

hook.text: Banks paid $321 billion in fines since 2008 but remain more profitable than ever.

buildup.text: After each scandal, banks promise culture change, hire compliance officers, and run ethics training.

discovery.text: Banking's core incentive — maximize short-term profits — conflicts with ethical behavior whenever ethics reduce revenue.

twist.text: Fintech disruption might force change. If customers can leave for transparent alternatives.

climax.text: Banking won't clean up from regulation alone. Real change requires customers who punish bad banks by leaving.

punchline.text: More fines, more reforms, more scandals.

quiz.question: What might finally force banks to change their behavior?

details.summary: Despite record fines, new regulations, and public outrage, banking scandals continue at a steady pace, suggesting that the profit incentives driving misconduct are more powerful than the penalties designed to stop it.
details.whyItMatters: If fines are just a cost of doing business, the current enforcement model is fundamentally broken. The persistence of scandals forces society to ask whether banking can ever be truly reformed.
takeaways: Banks have paid over $300 billion in fines since 2008
New scandals emerge regularly despite unprecedented regulation
Structural reforms may be more effective than fines alone

faq.question: Why aren't massive fines stopping bank misconduct?
faq.answer: Fines are typically a fraction of the profits generated by misconduct and are paid by shareholders, not executives. Until individuals face personal financial ruin or prison, fines function as a tax on bad behavior rather than a deterrent.

faq.question: What structural changes could actually clean up banking?
faq.answer: Separating risky trading from deposit-taking, requiring executives to personally forfeit bonuses after misconduct, and giving regulators the same compensation and resources as banks would create more alignment between behavior and consequences.
